title.narrative: Guaranteeing housing rights and climate justice for vulnerably housed women in São Paulo

description.narrative:
Over 2 million people in São Paulo metropolitan area live in inadequate and unsafe housing on the outskirts of the city in favelas and occupations, far from jobs, services and without basic infrastructure. At least 53,000 people are street homeless in central SP, whilst 600,000 people live in inadequate conditions in the city. High rents in both favelas and tenements leave little for daily sustenance, work travel of 4-5 hours/day leaves no time for family life.
Historic legacies of slavery, internal displacement and contemporary discrimination mean black and mixed-race people are most affected by urban inequality. Violent disputes for territorial control between drug gangs and/or police and increasing impacts of climate change and environmental degradation leave communities vulnerable to tragedy. Nevertheless, Brazil has a strong policy-framework and technical capacity, which if applied and adequately resourced could turn cities like São Paulo into engines of socioeconomic inclusion, environmental transformation and equality. Strengthening the organisation, know-how and networks of communities to claim their rights is essential to bringing this about.
This project will strengthen the voice, influence and organisation of approximately 10,000 vulnerably housed people from 45 grassroots housing organisations in order that they can shape the design and implementation of public policies for safe and permanent housing and neighbourhoods. The principal beneficiaries will be women, children and older people from predominantly black and mixed-race communities who will benefit from improved access to safe and permanent housing, reductions in environmental risks and access to urban services, including sanitation, electricity and sustainable transport. Communities in informal occupations of land and buildings in the centre and outskirts of São Paulo will be prioritised, who are at risk of eviction and violence and elevated exposure to environmental risks will be prioritised.
